Tutorial

This page is a guided Angular tutorial for building one complete feature with from the ground up. You will move step by step from project setup, to Feature State definition, to registration and initialization, and finally to a working UI that reads, selects, adds, and updates managed State.

By the end of the page, you will have a typed , an Angular service that owns the Feature boundary, a component that binds to reactive State, and a complete character workflow that can render, select, create, and update records from a managed collection.

Business Use Case
  • A product team needs a simple detail view that presents one record from a managed collection without exposing state-management mechanics in the component.
  • The feature must keep domain ownership in a service so UI code can stay focused on display logic, template binding, and user interaction.
  • The same structure should scale from a read-only detail screen to later workflows such as editing, validation, loading states, and testing without changing the core boundary.

Step 3: Define Feature State
↑ top

State is the feature-owned data that describes a feature at a specific moment. Defining State means deciding which values belong to the feature, assigning a type to each value, and identifying which properties are required.

In TypeScript, an interface captures those decisions as a compile-time contract for the and its consumers. This contract makes the expected State shape explicit, keeps State usage consistent, and allows TypeScript to identify missing properties and incompatible values during development. The interface defines the shape of State; it does not create or load a State value.

In , each declares State for a single Feature. This keeps the State definition focused on the data owned by that Feature instead of combining unrelated application data into one shared global store definition.

In this tutorial, the Feature and the State represents characters from the Star Wars universe.

Each character has an identifier, name, faction, and force-sensitive status. Keeping these fields in one focused State definition gives the , Pipeline, and Angular application a consistent representation of the character data.

Take Action
  1. Create a new file named: star-wars-character.shape.ts 
{{ starWarsCharacterStateSource.source }}
Global Store vs.

In a global store, all application data is combined into one shared State definition. This can lead to a large, complex State shape that is difficult to manage and maintain. In contrast, a defines State for a single Feature, keeping the State definition focused and manageable.

Tutorial 2

User-Directed Read Flow

The first tutorial established a minimal boundary for reading managed State. This next section keeps that same service-owned , but upgrades the UI from one fixed record to a user-selected read path.

The important shift is architectural, not mechanical: selection stays local to the component, while Feature State remains owned by the service. The result is a more interactive read experience without moving State ownership out of the existing boundary.

Step 11: Add a Dropdown
↑ top

This step upgrades the initial read path from showing the first committed record automatically to letting the user choose which committed record to inspect. The Feature registration, service-owned , and managed collection stay the same; only the UI-facing selection logic changes.

Assume the Angular mechanics are already familiar. The lesson here is narrower: keep Feature State in the service, keep selection state in the component, and derive the displayed record from the latest service-owned collection. To do that, replace the single displayed-character computed Signal with a read-only character collection, a selectedCharacterId Signal, a computed lookup for the selected record, and a small selection handler. In the template, add a select element that lists the registered characters and keep the detail panel bound to computed controller state instead of reaching into directly. The verification for this step belongs alongside that delta: the updated component spec should prove the controller starts empty, accepts a valid selection, ignores unknown ids, and renders the selected record without moving ownership out of the service.

Take Action
  1. Open example.component.ts.
  2. Expose the committed collection and add Signals for the selected character id and selected character.
  3. Add a method that maps the dropdown value to a known character id from the current -managed collection.
  4. Open example.component.html.
  5. Add a dropdown above the details panel and render an empty state until the user selects a character from the managed collection.
  6. Update example.component.spec.ts to verify both the empty state and the selected-record state.
What to Look For
  • The service still owns the and does not change for this UI enhancement.
  • The selection Signal is presentation state owned by the component, not Feature State owned by the service.
  • The template continues to render computed, display-ready values instead of reading APIs directly.
  • The spec verifies the new UI behavior without changing the -owned Feature State contract.

Tutorial 3

Add/Edit Mutation Flow

The dropdown tutorial proved that the same service-owned collection can support user-directed reads. This final section turns that read model into a mutation workflow by adding merge configuration, create behavior, and update behavior on top of the same boundary.

The teaching goal here is to keep mutation policy inside the pipeline and committed Feature State inside the service, while the component owns only local form, mode, and feedback state. That separation is what makes the add/edit slice extensible instead of ad hoc.

Step 13: Configure Array Append Merge
↑ top

Before the service can add a new character correctly, the registered needs append-style merge semantics. The default merge path replaces the existing array with the incoming array. That is correct for full replacement updates, but it is wrong for this tutorial's create flow because createCharacter() submits one new character through mergeState() and expects that record to be appended to the existing collection.

To change that Merge-stage behavior, install @sdux-vault/addons and register withArrayAppendMergeBehavior in app.config.ts. This makes mergeState() concatenate the incoming one-item array with the current committed collection, which is the exact behavior needed when adding a new character without replacing the others.

Take Action
  1. Install the @sdux-vault/addons package.
  2. Open app.config.ts.
  3. Import withArrayAppendMergeBehavior from @sdux-vault/addons.
  4. Pass [withArrayAppendMergeBehavior] as the behavior list for provide(). 
npm install @sdux-vault/addons
Why This Behavior Is Required
  • mergeState() is the right API for adding a new record to an existing collection.
  • Without array-append merge behavior, the incoming one-item array would replace the entire current collection.
  • With withArrayAppendMergeBehavior, that same one-item array is appended immutably to the committed collection.
  • This keeps add and edit distinct: create uses mergeState() to append, while update will use replaceState() to swap one existing character by identity. 
{{ addEditServiceFiles[0]?.source }}
Avoid Manual Array Merging

You could build the next collection manually with an old-school spread expression such as [...currentCharacters, newCharacter], but that is the wrong lesson for this tutorial.

The spread operator itself does not mutate the array. The anti-pattern is pushing merge policy into the service instead of configuring it in the pipeline. In , append behavior belongs to the Merge stage so mergeState() can apply that rule consistently instead of forcing application code to reimplement it by hand.

Step 14: Add the Add/Edit Service Slice
↑ top

This step turns the user-directed read example into the first mutation slice. The lesson is still the same: the service owns the , while the component owns only temporary editor state. What changes now is the write path. The service gains the create and update methods that mutate the registered collection, and a small domain helper keeps ID assignment and draft creation out of the Angular service body.

Assume the Angular form primitives are already familiar. Focus on the boundary: the service assigns IDs, routes creates through mergeState(), routes updates through replaceState(), and keeps every write inside the service instead of spreading mutation logic across the component and template.

Take Action
  1. Update example.service.ts to add the create and update methods.
  2. Keep the service as the only place that calls mutation APIs.
What to Look For
  • The service owns the write path just as completely as it owned the read path.
  • Create uses mergeState() because it appends a new record to the existing collection.
  • Update uses replaceState() because it replaces one existing record by identity.
  • The domain helper supports add/edit mechanics, but it does not own any behavior. The service still owns the .

Step 15: Complete Add/Edit Tutorial
↑ top

The add/edit tutorial is complete once the page can enter create mode, validate editor input, save a new character into the managed collection, and reopen an existing character for updates without moving Feature ownership out of the service. The collection picker, detail panel, and form now all react to the same -managed collection.

This is the first full CRUD-style expansion that still keeps the tutorial disciplined. The component gains form state, mode state, and feedback state, but the service remains the only place that creates or replaces Feature State. That is the important lesson: the service owns the , and the component owns only temporary UI state. The component does not call APIs directly, and it does not mutate the registered collection. The service remains the single source of truth for all Feature State. That is the boundary to preserve before a later destructive-action step adds deletion.

Take Action
  1. Update example.component.ts to add the form, editor mode, feedback state, and save/cancel flows.
  2. Update example.component.html to add the editor panel, the add action, and the empty-state guidance for create mode.
  3. Return to the running Angular application and verify that you can add a character, select it, edit it, and see the detail panel react to the saved State.
What Changed From the Dropdown Example
  • The component now owns local editor state in addition to local selection state.
  • The template adds a form and feedback region, but it still does not call APIs directly.
  • Saving a new record and saving an edited record both flow through the same service-owned .
  • Delete is still intentionally absent so this slice can focus on non-destructive mutation only.
